content: Nocturnal enuresis, commonly known as bedwetting, is a socially challenging and emotionally distressing condition that affects approximately 15% to 20% of five-year-old children and persists in up to 2% of young adults. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of complementary interventions, as well as other approaches such as surgery or dietary modifications, on nocturnal enuresis in children. It also sought to compare these interventions with other established treatments. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including PubMed, EMBASE, TCMLARS, CBM, CNKI, and the VIP database, covering literature up to June 2010. No language restrictions were applied. The study included all randomized or quasi-randomized trials that investigated complementary and miscellaneous interventions for nocturnal enuresis in children, excluding those focused solely on daytime wetting. Comparison interventions included no treatment, placebo or sham treatments, alarms, simple behavioral therapies, desmopressin, imipramine, and other miscellaneous drugs or interventions. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the eligible trials and extracted data. A total of 24 randomized controlled trials involving 2334 children were included, with 1283 children receiving a complementary intervention. However, the overall quality of the trials was poor. Five trials were quasi-randomized, five showed baseline differences between groups, and 17 lacked follow-up data. In one trial, hypnosis demonstrated better outcomes than imipramine, with a lower risk of failure or relapse after stopping treatment (relative risk [RR] 0.42, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.23 to 0.78). Psychotherapy appeared to be more effective than both alarm therapy (RR 0.28, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.85) and reward-based interventions (RR 0.29, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.90) in reducing the number of children who failed or relapsed, but this conclusion was based on data from a single trial. One trial suggested that medicinal herbs were more effective than desmopressin, with a lower risk of failure or relapse after treatment cessation (RR 0.35, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.85). Acupuncture was found to be superior to sham acupuncture in another trial, with a reduced risk of failure or relapse after stopping treatment (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.94). Active chiropractic adjustments also showed better results than sham adjustments in one trial (RR for failure to improve 0.76, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.95). However, all these findings were derived from small, single trials, and their reliability is limited. The evidence for dietary interventions and faradization was deemed unreliable, and no trials were identified that investigated homeopathy or surgical interventions. In conclusion, there is weak evidence supporting the use of hypnosis, psychotherapy, acupuncture, chiropractic adjustments, and medicinal herbs for the treatment of nocturnal enuresis in children. However, these findings are based on small, methodologically questionable trials. Further robust randomized controlled trials are necessary to establish the efficacy, cost-effectiveness, and safety of these interventions.
